title: Raga Jaijavanti
hookLine: where the Granth's ragas end, one voice sings alone: Guru Tegh Bahadur, and a kingdom built like a wall of sand

lines: A WALL PATTED SMOOTH WITH BOTH HANDS.
ONE VOICE, AND A WALL OF SAND.
cards: A sandcastle at the edge of the tide can be a fine thing: towers, a moat, a wall patted smooth with both hands. Everyone on the beach knows how the story ends, and still somebody builds it.
The Guru Granth Sahib's long run of ragas has gone from evening to dawn and back.
Today it reaches the place where the ragas end, a section called Jaijavanti that holds a single voice, and in its first hymn, a wall made of sand.

teach.b: Jaijavanti follows Prabhati, and it is the last of the raga sections in the Granth's order. After it come verses gathered without a raga heading, and at the very end a page that comes up in two days.

Jaijavanti is short, and every hymn in it is by Guru Tegh Bahadur. Tradition says his hymns were added to the Granth by his son, Guru Gobind Singh. In many ragas, voices take turns: Gurus, then Bhagats.
Here one voice sings alone, the way a concert sometimes ends with a single singer.
The first hymn opens with a doubled call, in paraphrase: remember the Lord, remember the Lord; this alone is your work. Leave clinging to Maya, the world's glitter, and take shelter with God.
Count the world's pleasures as false; the whole show is false. Then two pictures. Wealth is like riches in a dream.

teach.h: A KINGDOM LIKE A WALL OF SAND.
teach.b: And the rule of the whole earth is like a wall of sand. Hear how gently that's put. The hymn doesn't sneer at wealth or power.
A dream can be vivid; a sand wall can be well made. The point is what they're made of, and how long they stand. Against that, one thing is named as your work: remembering.
Remembering the One, twice over, so you hear it.
After all the moods, morning and evening, spring and rain, the last raga sets down a plain instruction.

how: Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns in Raga Jaijavanti are sung in kirtan, and Sikh tradition remembers him as the Guru who gave his life for others' freedom of faith.

o: the first raga of the Granth, sung in the early evening
the last raga section, holding Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymns alone
a long hymn by Kabir that closes every evening service

games.q: what's inside Raga Jaijavanti — tap the pairs.

s: Jaijavanti mixes the hymns of many Gurus and Bhagats
every hymn in it is by Guru Tegh Bahadur.
Jaijavanti is the last raga section in the Granth's order
after it come verses without a raga heading.
the hymn sneers at wealth and power
it calls them a dream and a wall of sand, and names remembering as your work.

games.q: the ragas are ending. you're Guru Tegh Bahadur, and you have one hymn to open the last section. what do you call 'your work'?
o: leaving the world for the forest.
games.why: the hymn opens: remember the Lord, remember the Lord; this alone is your work.

practice: If you can, play a shabad of Guru Tegh Bahadur sung in Raga Jaijavanti; if not, sit in the quiet and bring to mind one thing you've been building lately, a savings goal, a reputation, a project, and without judging it, notice what it's made of.
Then let it rest, the way you'd leave a sandcastle on the beach, and stay with the breath, as if remembering were your only job.
If you pray, let the doubled call, remember the Lord, sit on the breath; if you don't, come back to breathing each time the building starts again.

wordCard.voice: Raga Jaijavanti. The last raga section of the Granth, holding hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur alone, which opens: remember the Lord, remember; this alone is your work. Today's word.

orig.note: the last raga's name as it appears in the Granth's heading, Raag Jaijavanti.

carryVoice: Your line: the last raga. One voice sings alone, with one plain instruction: remember. Until tomorrow.
